question: Can reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards avoid reasoning-mode collapse by jointly rewarding diversity across correct trajectories and maintaining token-level entropy around the most distinctive correct modes?

key_findings.claim: Author method: DSDR gives correct rollouts a clipped global-diversity bonus built from semantic dissimilarity and formula uniqueness, so solve-all groups retain nonconstant rewards.
key_findings.evidence: Each response is embedded with frozen all-MiniLM-L6-v2; its mean pairwise cosine distance is averaged with the fraction of extracted formulas unique within the rollout group. The resulting d(o_i) is clipped at sigma-d and added only when the verifier reward is one. This directly makes rewards differ in an all-correct group if the diversity scores differ, but exact formula matching and a small sentence encoder are unvalidated proxies for genuinely different reasoning.

key_findings.claim: Author method: local exploration is a positive-only, length-normalized entropy objective whose budget is allocated across correct rollouts by a softmax of their global distinctiveness.
key_findings.evidence: Weights w_i are proportional to exp(tau times clipped diversity) over correct responses and zero otherwise. The local term reuses behavior-policy tokens with importance ratio rho, averages negative rho log pi over response length, and multiplies by w_i. Maximizing it raises per-token entropy most around globally distinctive correct trajectories. If no rollout is correct, both the global bonus and local mechanism are inactive.

anchors.section: 3.2.2-3.2.3 global-to-local coupling and local positive-sample regularization

key_findings.claim: Author-reported main result: DSDR improves the average Pass@1 and Avg@16 columns over Backbone, GRPO, and DAPO at all three reported model scales.
key_findings.evidence: For Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, the average rises to 25.4/25.6 versus 23.2/24.0 for the strongest GRPO baseline; for Qwen3-1.7B it reaches 36.8/36.8 versus DAPO's 29.6/32.1; for Qwen3-4B it reaches 48.01/46.80 versus DAPO's 38.94/40.21 and GRPO's 39.31/39.57. The largest gains occur on AIME24/25. These are single reported point estimates with no run-level uncertainty.

anchors.section: Appendix A training and evaluation settings

key_findings.claim: Author-reported ablation: global diversity and global-to-local coupling are complementary on average, although individual cells do not uniformly favor the complete method.
key_findings.evidence: On Qwen3-1.7B, removing global diversity lowers the average from 36.8/36.8 to 29.7/31.4 and removing coupling lowers it to 35.1/34.9. On Qwen3-4B, the corresponding variants score 44.14/43.76 and 32.04/41.20 versus 48.01/46.80. Yet w/o coupling slightly exceeds full DSDR on 1.7B Minerva Pass@1 (23.5 versus 23.3) and Olympiad Avg@16 (36.1 versus 36.0), so the evidence supports average complementarity rather than universal per-task necessity.

anchors.section: Table 1 w/o GD and w/o GC rows / 4.3 Ablation Study

key_findings.claim: Author-reported exploration result: DSDR improves Pass@k curves and an LLM-judged diversity score relative to selected baselines, but Avg@16 itself is only mean correctness and is not evidence of mode diversity.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 3 reports DSDR above Base and DAPO for k from 2 through 64 on five math benchmarks, with wider gaps on AIME and Olympiad and smaller absolute gains on Minerva. Figure 5 uses GPT-5.2 to judge 32 rollouts per problem on semantic, logical, and formula diversity and compares DSDR with DAPO; DSDR is higher in diversity and Pass@32 on four benchmarks. The figures provide no tabulated values or judge uncertainty, and GRPO and direct diversity competitors are absent from the judge comparison.

anchors.section: Evaluation Setting definitions of Avg@16 and Pass@k

key_findings.claim: Author-reported negative result: excessive local entropy destabilizes training and collapses performance, so the usable regularization range is narrow and tuned.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4.6 says local coefficients above 0.01 cause instability and collapse; lambda-l=0.001 is selected. Lambda-d=0.001 is also chosen because larger global bonuses add variance without consistent gains, and tau=5 is selected from {1,5,10}. The main results therefore depend on a three-way sweep, not a parameter-free principle.

anchors.section: Appendix A hyperparameter grids and Tables 2-3

key_findings.claim: Author theory with a strong boundary: bounded entropy preserves optimal correctness only if the policy class has a strictly positive gap between optimal and all suboptimal correctness values.
key_findings.evidence: The inter-/intra-mode identity decomposes output entropy into mutual information with a latent mode and within-mode entropy. Proposition C.2 then shows any maximizer of J_R plus lambda-l J_H is correctness-optimal when lambda-l is smaller than Delta/log|V|. The result assumes Delta=J-star-R minus the best strictly suboptimal value is positive; the appendix notes this may hold for a restricted discrete policy class, but a continuously parameterized LLM policy can admit arbitrarily close suboptimal values. It also proves a population optimum statement, not that finite GRPO training preserves accuracy.

anchors.section: C.2 entropy decomposition and C.3 correctness preservation

key_findings.claim: Author theory: nonconstant correct-only bonuses prevent zero normalized advantages in solve-all groups, and diversity-softmax uniquely solves a maximum-entropy allocation problem.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma C.3 gives the mixed binary-reward group probability 1-p^G-(1-p)^G. Proposition C.4 observes that if augmented rewards differ, their variance is positive and stabilized normalized advantages are not all zero. Proposition C.5 derives weights proportional to exp(tau d_i) as the unique optimizer of tau E_w[d] plus allocation entropy. These are mathematically valid but limited: C.4 is a nondegeneracy statement, not proof that the resulting direction is unbiased or improves exploration, and C.5 justifies a chosen allocation objective rather than deriving that objective from task performance.

anchors.section: C.4 Lemma C.3 and Proposition C.4

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: Theorem 3.1 does not exactly derive the implemented coupling because it treats diversity as a property of one rollout, whereas both implemented global signals depend on the entire sampled group.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 6-9 define D_emb(o_i) by comparisons with every o_j and formula uniqueness relative to the union of other responses. Theorem 3.1 instead assumes a fixed scalar d(q,o) inside a single-rollout expectation and applies the one-sample score-function identity. For an actual set-dependent score, the objective is an expectation over the joint group; its gradient contains the sum of all rollout log-probability gradients and cross-rollout effects. The appendix proof does not show that the per-response weights in Equation 20 are the gradient estimator of that group objective.

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: the implementation report contains two smaller configuration inconsistencies that impede exact reproduction.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4.1 says training uses four base models but names only Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-4B, the same three blocks shown in Table 1. Section 4.6 says lambda-l values larger than 0.01 caused collapse, while Appendix A lists the local sweep only as {0.001, 0.002, 0.01}; no tested above-0.01 values are disclosed there. These look like reporting omissions rather than evidence against the main result, but they prevent a complete audit of model count and sensitivity.

key_findings.claim: Reviewer inference: DSDR's credible novelty is the explicit allocation of token-level entropy according to correct trajectory distinctiveness, not diversity-aware RLVR itself.
key_findings.evidence: Prior methods already optimize positive-sample token diversity, sequence-level semantic diversity, DPP set diversity, and Pass@k utility. DSDR combines a lightweight embedding/formula bonus with positive-only entropy and ties them through a softmax over correct group members. The benchmark gains support this engineering combination on small math models, while the theoretical derivation mismatch, strict correctness-gap assumption, incomplete uncertainty reporting, and same-task hyperparameter selection leave general causal and policy-optimality claims open.

method.core_idea: Coordinate two kinds of correctness-aligned exploration in group-based RLVR: reward correct trajectories for being globally distinct, then spend a length-normalized token-entropy budget preferentially around the most distinct correct trajectories.
method.mechanism: For each prompt, DSDR samples eight rollouts and assigns binary verifier rewards. It embeds complete responses with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, computes mean pairwise cosine distance, extracts formulas and scores their within-group uniqueness, and averages the two signals. A clipped diversity bonus augments only correct rewards before GRPO normalization. A softmax over clipped diversity among correct rollouts produces allocation weights. The local objective uses behavior-policy importance ratios and negative current-policy log probability, averaged over tokens and weighted by that allocation. Experiments train Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and Qwen3 1.7B/4B on filtered DAPO-Math-17K and evaluate five math suites.
assumptions: Cosine distance in all-MiniLM-L6-v2 space reflects distinct mathematical reasoning modes rather than surface phrasing.
Formula extraction is reliable and exact set uniqueness captures symbolic strategy differences.
A simple average of semantic and formula scores puts the two notions on comparable, calibrated scales.
Diversity should be rewarded only on verifier-correct trajectories, and no diversity signal is needed for an all-incorrect prompt group.
Clipping and a small lambda-d prevent semantic or formula reward hacking without suppressing useful variation.
Mean per-token entropy is a useful proxy for intra-mode diversity and removes length incentives.
The off-policy importance ratio yields a stable entropy estimate under the PPO/GRPO update regime.
More globally distinctive correct trajectories deserve more local entropy than common correct trajectories.
A softmax allocation objective based on diversity plus allocation entropy is aligned with downstream exploration quality.
The positive correctness gap required by Proposition C.2 is meaningful for the practical neural policy class.
A group-relative diversity score can be treated as a single-rollout scalar in the policy-gradient derivation.
Five competition-math benchmarks and three models up to 4B characterize broader reasoning exploration.

Uses 64 test-time samples to trace the probability of at least one correct response across k.

limitations: Author-stated: formula diversity is set to zero when no formula is detected, an intentionally conservative choice that makes the global signal task-format dependent.
Author-stated: diversity bonuses are clipped and restricted to correct rollouts to reduce reward hacking; this acknowledges that the learned proxies can otherwise dominate correctness.
Author-stated: gains on Minerva are modest because correct solutions are sparse.
Author-stated: local coefficients above 0.01 are reported to destabilize and collapse training, while larger global coefficients introduce variance without consistent gains.
Author-stated: correctness preservation requires a strict positive gap between optimal and all suboptimal attainable correctness and sufficiently small regularization.
Author-stated: Theorem 3.1 assumes the diversity-tilted normalizer Z is positive, so it does not cover prompts with zero probability of a correct rollout.
Reviewer-identified: both DSDR signals vanish for an all-incorrect group, precisely where difficult prompts may need exploration most.
Reviewer-identified: the single-rollout policy-gradient theorem does not match the implementation's group-dependent pairwise and uniqueness scores.
Reviewer-identified: the experiments report no independent seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or prompt-level paired analysis.

Reviewer-identified: all training uses one filtered 17K math dataset and evaluations cover five math suites; no code, science, multimodal, instruction-following, or distribution-shift training evaluation establishes broad reasoning transfer.
Reviewer-identified: models stop at 4B parameters, and results do not test whether the mechanism persists at frontier RLVR scale.
Reviewer-identified: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings can reward paraphrase or stylistic distance and miss mathematically distinct but semantically similar derivations.
Reviewer-identified: exact formula set uniqueness is brittle to algebraic equivalence, formatting, extraction errors, and repeated boilerplate.
Reviewer-identified: the GPT-5.2 diversity comparison uses an LLM judge, only DAPO as comparator, no judge repeats or calibration, and no tabulated numbers.
Reviewer-identified: Avg@16 is average sample correctness rather than a set-level diversity metric, so it cannot support mode-coverage claims by itself.
Reviewer-identified: the paper does not quantify embedding, formula parsing, or pairwise group-scoring overhead relative to RL rollout and verifier cost.
Reviewer-identified: hyperparameters are selected on AIME24/25-style performance without a clearly separated validation protocol, risking benchmark-adaptive tuning.
Reviewer-identified: Section 4.1's four-model statement and Appendix A's incomplete above-0.01 local sweep impede exact reproduction.
Reviewer-identified: Proposition C.4 only proves a nonzero normalized advantage when bonuses differ; it does not prove the new advantage is low variance, unbiased for correctness, or beneficial.
Reviewer-identified: no direct comparison with DIVER, Diversity-Aware Policy Optimization, DARLING, DQO, or PKPO isolates novelty against current diversity-specific RL methods.
failure_modes: When all sampled responses are incorrect, DSDR supplies no global bonus and no local entropy, so the policy receives no new exploration mechanism.
A stylistically unusual but substantively redundant correct response can earn a large embedding bonus.
Algebraically equivalent formulas written differently can be counted as unique, while genuinely distinct derivations using the same formulas can be counted as identical.
A small immediate verifier-correct set can make the diversity-softmax allocation noisy and concentrate the whole entropy budget on an outlier.
High lambda-l can increase random token entropy, destabilize clipping, and erase correctness.
A global diversity bonus can change which correct modes dominate without improving coverage of unsolved prompts.
Importance ratios can become unstable when current and behavior policies drift, especially on long 8K responses.
Per-token averaging can hide a short region of severe entropy collapse or over-randomization inside a long solution.
The group-dependent score can induce cross-sample policy-gradient terms omitted by the stated estimator.
Reward hacking can target formatting, formula proliferation, or semantic-embedding distance rather than new solution strategies.
LLM-judge diversity can favor verbosity and presentation differences even when pass@k gains come from ordinary accuracy improvement.
A correctness-gap guarantee can fail for continuous policies whose expected accuracy approaches the optimum arbitrarily closely.
reusable_insights: Separate trajectory-level mode coverage from within-mode token variability instead of treating entropy as a complete diversity metric.
Restrict exploratory bonuses to verified solutions when incorrect novelty would otherwise be rewarded, but separately address all-incorrect groups.
Normalize token entropy by response length to avoid rewarding longer chains solely for accumulating uncertainty.
Allocate local exploration using a transparent simplex optimization and report the temperature's effective concentration.
Evaluate diversity methods with Pass@1, Pass@k, calibrated set-diversity metrics, and per-prompt uncertainty rather than one aggregate accuracy.
Ablate global reward shaping and local entropy separately and report every per-task reversal, not just average gains.
When a reward feature depends on a sampled set, derive the policy gradient for the joint set distribution rather than substituting a single-response score.
Test semantic-diversity rewards against paraphrase, formula-equivalence, verbosity, and adversarial formatting controls.
Use a held-out tuning suite for diversity coefficients because the stable range can be narrow.
Measure how often groups are all wrong, mixed, or all correct; the utility of correct-only shaping depends directly on those regimes.
open_questions: How can correct-mode exploration be encouraged on prompts for which an entire rollout group is initially wrong?
Does a joint-policy-gradient derivation for group-relative diversity yield the same DSDR update or require cross-rollout terms?
Would a learned mathematical-equivalence model outperform exact formula uniqueness without introducing exploitable judge bias?
How much of the gain comes from making all-correct GRPO rewards nonconstant versus genuinely discovering new reasoning modes?
Does DSDR outperform direct current diversity methods under identical backbones, rollout budgets, and verifier pipelines?
Do the gains persist across seeds and at 7B, 32B, and mixture-of-experts scales?
Can the strict correctness-gap theorem be replaced by a guarantee for continuous neural policy classes or approximate stationary points?
How sensitive are results to sentence encoder, embedding dimension, formula parser, group size, and score clipping?
Does diversity learned on competition math improve code, theorem proving, scientific reasoning, or out-of-domain compositional tasks?
Can human or equivalence-checked annotations confirm that lower embedding similarity corresponds to distinct valid solution strategies?
What are the memory and runtime costs of all-pairs response embeddings and formula comparison during large-scale RLVR?
Which undisclosed lambda-l values above 0.01 were tested, and can the reported collapse be reproduced?

competitive_landscape.title: Diversity-Aware Policy Optimization for Large Language Model Reasoning
competitive_landscape.difference: Diversity-Aware Policy Optimization already defines token-level diversity, applies it selectively to positive samples, and reports a 3.5-point average math gain. DSDR adds an explicit trajectory-level embedding/formula reward and uses that global score to allocate the local entropy budget. Its novelty relative to this prior is the cross-scale coupling, not positive-only token diversity.

competitive_landscape.title: Diversity-Incentivized Exploration for Versatile Reasoning
competitive_landscape.difference: DIVER already uses sequence-level semantic diversity as an intrinsic RLVR reward, reports Pass@1/Pass@k and out-of-domain gains, and uses potential-based shaping to preserve optimal-policy invariance. DSDR's narrower addition is a positive-only token-entropy term whose allocation depends on global distinctiveness. The current paper does not empirically compare against DIVER, and its strict-gap correctness theorem is not obviously stronger than DIVER's policy-invariance framing.

competitive_landscape.title: Jointly Reinforcing Diversity and Quality in Language Model Generations
competitive_landscape.difference: DARLING already combines a learned partition-based semantic diversity signal with quality reward in online RL and demonstrates both creative-task and verifiable-math gains. DSDR uses cheaper pairwise embeddings plus formula uniqueness, confines rewards and entropy to correct math trajectories, and explicitly couples sequence and token scales. Its evidence is narrower in task breadth but more specific to group-normalized RLVR.

competitive_landscape.title: Post-training Large Language Models for Diverse High-Quality Responses
competitive_landscape.difference: DQO treats a response group as a set and optimizes DPP kernel volume for quality plus semantic diversity across instruction following, summarization, stories, and reasoning. DSDR instead decomposes a per-response group score and a token entropy term. The set-dependent nature of DQO also highlights the gap in DSDR's single-rollout policy-gradient derivation; DSDR's distinct contribution is the global-to-local allocation rule.

competitive_landscape.title: Pass@K Policy Optimization: Solving Harder Reinforcement Learning Problems
competitive_landscape.difference: PKPO directly derives low-variance unbiased estimators for arbitrary Pass@k and transforms group rewards to optimize collective sample utility, with annealing to retain Pass@1. DSDR optimizes heuristic semantic/formula diversity and reports Pass@k only as evaluation. DSDR uniquely targets within-mode entropy, while PKPO has the cleaner direct connection to the set-level success metric.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Correctness-aligned exploration requires dual-scale diversity: global rewards preserve multiple correct reasoning modes, positive length-invariant entropy prevents collapse within modes, and a principled global-to-local softmax coupling yields stronger and more stable RLVR.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper defines bounded semantic/formula bonuses, correct-only reward shaping, positive-sample importance-weighted entropy, and diversity-based allocation; reports Pass@1/Avg@16 improvements at three model scales, ablations of global diversity and coupling, Pass@k curves, training dynamics, an LLM-judge comparison, and several theoretical propositions about entropy decomposition, correctness gaps, advantage nondegeneracy, and softmax allocation.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: After positive-token diversity, global semantic intrinsic rewards, learned semantic partitioning, DPP set diversity, and direct Pass@k optimization, the defensible novelty is the explicit softmax allocation of local token entropy according to each correct trajectory's group-level distinctiveness. The average math gains are substantial, especially at 1.7B and 4B, but the causal and generality claims are narrower than presented: no current diversity-specific competitor is run, point estimates lack uncertainty, all-incorrect groups receive no help, the correctness result needs a strict unattested gap, and Theorem 3.1 does not derive the actual group-dependent diversity estimator. The incomplete model-count and hyperparameter reports further reduce reproducibility confidence.
